title: New privacy rules for Google's Gemini Apps (updated November 16, 2026)
content:
Last updated: November 16, 2026
Gemini Apps Privacy Notice
Last updated: November 16, 2026
This notice supplements the Google Privacy Policy, and they explain how Google processes your data when you interact with Gemini, your personal AI assistant from Google, through the services listed here (“Gemini Apps” or “Gemini” for short) while signed in. The Google Privacy Policy explains how Google processes your data when you use Gemini while you’re signed out.
Gemini Apps are provided by Google Ireland Limited in the European Economic Area and Switzerland and by Google LLC everywhere else. We refer to both companies as "Google" below.
Information you provide Gemini Apps
- What you say to Gemini Apps (like the prompts you submit or speak, and tasks you ask Gemini to do)
- What you share with Gemini Apps (like files, videos, screens you ask about, photos, imported chats, and page content you share from your browser)
- Transcripts and recordings of your interactions with Gemini Live
- Your feedback
- Instructions you provide, for example, in Gems and Skills as well as Instructions for Gemini (“Saved Info”in some locales)
Information we collect as you use Gemini Apps
- Content that Gemini Apps generates (like text, code, audio, images, video, music, public links, citations, chat summaries, and personalized insights)
- Information about steps our technologies take to do tasks for you or respond to your prompts, like model thinking steps, trajectory info, and tool calls
- Information from your apps, browsers, and devices 
    
  - Information from your Connected Apps (including third-party services such as Model Context Protocol server tools) and other Google services you use with Gemini Apps (such as your Search or YouTube history, or your page context and URL from Chrome)
  - Information about the apps on your device (for example, to help you get things done using your apps)
  - Information about the apps, browsers, and devices you use to access Gemini Apps (such as identifiers, browser type and settings, device type and settings, operating system)
  - Interaction of your apps, browsers, and devices with Gemini Apps (such as interaction logs, performance metrics, crash and debug information)
  - System permissions and device data when you use Gemini mobile apps, such as call and message logs, contacts (to help you keep in touch), installed apps (like Clock), language preferences (to help you speak to Gemini), screen content (to help you act on it), and other app info like page context and URL (when you use Gemini overlay to ask questions)
  - Remote browser data like cookies that contain your website authentication info and screen captures or other page content
  - Remote computer data like executed code and processed files
  - Context info from devices and services you use with Gemini (such as smart home device names and playlists)
  - Data about your interactions with public Gemini Apps content
- Supplemental information: information collected through supplemental Gemini Apps features you choose to use.
- Location information: the general area from your device, IP address, or Home or Work addresses in your Google Account, and saved history. Learn more at g.co/privacypolicy/location.
- Subscription information: if you have a paid subscription to a Google AI plan, subscription related information.
Google uses this data, as described in our Privacy Policy, to:
- Provide our services
- Maintain and improve our services
- Develop new services
- Personalize our services
- Customize our services
- Communicate with you
- Measure performance
- Protect Google, our users, and the public
These uses extend to the generative AI models and other machine-learning technologies powering our services.
Human reviewers (including trained reviewers from our service providers) review some of the data we collect for these purposes. Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.
- We rely on other Google services and infrastructure to provide Gemini Apps. For example, some Gemini responses are grounded on Search results. Gemini also relies on some Google settings, for example, Gemini can help you hands-free based on your “Hey Google” & Voice Match settings.
- If you are 18 or older and upgrade to Gemini Apps, your calling or texting history may be imported from your Web & App Activity to Gemini History in some regions. This helps improve your Gemini Apps experience, like contact suggestions. Learn more.
Gemini Apps work with Connected Apps, including Google apps and third-party services. Gemini saves and uses info from Connected Apps according to this notice, including to provide and improve Gemini Apps. Connected Google apps save and use your data, per their policies and the Google Privacy Policy, including to provide and improve their services. If you use Gemini Apps to interact with third-party services, they process your data according to their own privacy policies.
Eligible users with Personal Intelligence can connect some Google apps to Gemini Apps to get new, more personalized experiences. Learn more about eligibility.
Gemini Apps may activate when you didn’t intend them to, for example, if there’s a noise that sounds like “Hey Google” or if you activate them accidentally by touch. If Gemini Apps respond, they will treat your input like a normal activation. Depending on your settings, this data is used to improve Google services. These include Gemini models, other generative AI models that power Gemini Apps, and technologies that help reduce unintended activations.
When you interact with a user-generated Canvas app, the creator of the app can see any data you share and can save it where they choose. Google provides storage for Canvas app data in Firebase, but the app creator can also save your data elsewhere. Anyone with the public link can also view and edit data saved with the app. Be cautious and only share data with Canvas apps you trust.
You can visit your Google Account to manage your data and privacy. Gemini Apps also provide settings to help you manage your data and experience, like:
- Visit Gemini History to review and delete your history (including any imported chats), change your auto-delete period, and control whether your data is used to train generative AI models. Your Gemini settings don’t control processing of your chats to create anonymized data to improve Google services. Even if your settings do not allow generative AI model training on your chat content, Google still uses your chats to respond to you and help protect Google, our users, and the public, including with help from human reviewers. Learn how to manage your settings in Gemini History.
- Manage Gems and Skills in the Gems Manager and Skills Manager.
- Manage public links in Your Public Links.
- Manage Gemini Apps’ access to other apps and data (including third-party services such as Model Context Protocol server tools) in Connected Apps settings.
- Manage info you have asked Gemini to save.
- Manage your Task settings (including any linked phone numbers).
- Learn more about how to manage personalization features, including personalization with Memory and Personal Intelligence.
- You can use Gemini, hosted by the Google app, as your device assistant on Android. Learn more about how to manage your Google app permissions (such as device location, microphone, notification permissions, and camera permissions).
- Learn more about how to manage your Gemini mobile app settings.
- Learn more about how to set the Google app as the default digital assistant app.
If you change your Gemini Apps settings, other Google settings won’t change. Those settings, like Search Services History, Web & App Activity, or Timeline, may keep saving location and other data as you use other Google services.
We retain your data for different periods of time, depending on what it is and how we use it, as exp

report.summary: Google's updated Gemini privacy notice spells out expansive data collection — prompts, files, device context, model reasoning traces — plus human review, and the controls users have over history and training.
report.background: Privacy notices for AI assistants have shifted from boilerplate to substantive disclosure as regulators scrutinise them. Under GDPR in Europe (where Google Ireland is the data controller) and the EU AI Act's transparency obligations, providers must now be explicit about what an assistant captures, how long it is kept, and whether humans look at it. Google's own history raised the stakes: 2019 reporting revealed contractors listening to Google Assistant recordings, prompting a wave of opt-outs. Since then Gemini has evolved from a chatbot into an agentic layer spanning Chrome page context, Android device permissions, smart-home devices and third-party connections via Model Context Protocol servers. That expansion means the privacy notice now governs screen contents, executed code, cookies and tool calls — data categories far beyond typed prompts — making the November 16, 2026 revision a map of how much surface area a modern assistant touches.
key_points: The notice separates what you hand over (prompts, voice, files, videos, screenshots, imported chats, Gemini Live transcripts, custom Gems and Skills instructions) from what is collected passively: generated output, model thinking steps, trajectory data, tool calls, Chrome page context and URLs, cookies with site authentication, plus device permissions such as contacts, call logs and screen content.

Human reviewers — including staff at service providers — read some of the collected data for service improvement and safety. Google explicitly warns users not to enter confidential material they wouldn't want a reviewer to see, which undercuts any assumption that chats are private by default.

Turning off model-training in Gemini History does not stop all uses: Google still processes chats to answer you, to protect users and the public, and to produce anonymized data for improving services. Settings in Gemini don't propagate to other Google products like Web & App Activity or Timeline.

Third-party and user-generated surfaces carry separate risk. Canvas apps built by other users can see and store whatever you share, and anyone with a public link may view or edit that data; MCP server tools and other Connected Apps fall under their own privacy policies.

Accidental activations count as real input. If a noise resembling 'Hey Google' or a stray touch wakes Gemini, the response is treated like a normal request and may be used to improve models, including systems meant to reduce false wakes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this notice sets a disclosure template competitors will be measured against: enumerating reasoning traces and tool calls as personal data is a meaningful precedent, since it implies agent internals are discoverable and potentially reviewable. For developers, the sharpest signal is architectural — building on MCP servers or Canvas means inheriting data-handling obligations you don't control, and enterprise buyers will now ask harder questions about where prompts and screen captures land. For regular users, the practical takeaway is that consent is granular but fragmented: history auto-delete, training opt-outs, Connected Apps permissions and device-level grants must each be managed separately, and none of them make confidential input safe from human review. Convenience rises, but so does the cost of inattention.
report.tools: Follow Google's Gemini Apps Activity and auto-delete settings, My Activity, and Google Takeout for auditing or exporting data. For MCP, watch the open specification and reference servers plus clients like Claude Desktop and Cursor, and review Connected Apps permissions regularly. Privacy-conscious users can compare against local runners such as Ollama or LM Studio, and track enforcement news via the EDPB, Ireland's DPC and national data-protection authorities.
